text: Last lesson of Chapter 4: comparing two entire result sets against each other, not row by row with a join, but as whole sets at once.

Vendor ID where invoice date is in 2026, UNION, vendor ID where invoice date is before 2026. UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result. UNION ALL skips that step entirely — faster, and the one you should default to whenever duplicates can't occur or don't matter.

Same two queries, but MINUS instead of UNION. Every vendor ID that invoiced in 2026 but never invoiced before — new suppliers, from the data's perspective. Other databases call this EXCEPT; Oracle has always called it MINUS, and that's the name you'll see in existing Oracle Financials code.
Flip the operator one more time to INTERSECT, and you get suppliers who invoiced both before and during 2026 — established, ongoing relationships, not brand new ones.

Chapter 4 gave you the tools for questions that depend on another question's answer: subqueries, CTEs for naming and chaining logic, NOT EXISTS for what's missing, ROW_NUMBER for duplicates, and now set operators for comparing two results outright.
Chapter 4 complete. Next: Chapter 5, where every one of these tools gets put to work on real finance investigations — including, finally, the full unpaid-invoices challenge.
